query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small concentration of boron (≈1–2 at%) during alloy processing will segregate to the grain boundaries of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38, thereby increasing its load-bearing integrity without significantly altering its magneto- and pressure-caloric performance.
generation.material_initial_state: The current high-entropy alloy is homogeneous but exhibits brittle behavior with poor fracture toughness despite having a large caloric response.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with 1–2 atomic percent boron during melting and subsequent processing to promote grain boundary enrichment.
generation.conditions: Test conditions include operating under magnetic fields and pressure regimes typical for caloric operation, with temperatures near the thermal phase transition responsible for the caloric effect and mechanical loads that previously led to cracking.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron enrichment at the grain boundaries, which strengthens intergranular cohesion and limits the initiation and propagation of cracks.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms preferentially segregate to grain boundaries, reducing boundary energy and enhancing grain boundary strength. This grain-boundary reinforcement minimizes crack initiation under mechanical stress while the bulk phase transition that governs the caloric effect remains largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy is expected to exhibit improved fracture toughness and load-bearing capacity with minimal change (within about 10% of the original value) in the magnitude of the caloric effects under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
generation.baseline: The original alloy shows a strong caloric response but suffers from brittle failure due to poor load-bearing integrity.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under typical magnetic field intensities, pressure ranges, and mechanical loads encountered during caloric operation at temperatures near the phase transition. Extreme deviations from these conditions have not been tested.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the boron addition might subtly alter the phase transition characteristics that underlie the caloric response; precise optimization of boron content and processing parameters may be required to avoid trade-offs between mechanical and caloric performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with 1–2 at% boron doping and one set of control samples without boron. Process them identically. Subject both sets to mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness, stress–strain measurements) and evaluate their caloric performance through magneto-caloric and pressure-caloric measurements near the phase transition temperature.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC) and load-bearing stress measurements
Adiabatic temperature change (ΔT_ad) under an applied magnetic field
Isothermal entropy change (ΔS) under applied pressure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the boron-doped alloy fails to show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., <10% increase in fracture toughness relative to control) or if the caloric response is reduced by more than approximately 10% compared to the undoped alloy under the same operating conditions.
